summary: Direction: mixed — the most legally protective jurisdiction in Latin America, with a repeating pattern of police round-ups of travestis and trans women in one neighbourhood. The city has operated its own anti-discrimination law since 1996, hosts a large visible scene and an LGBTQ-driven tourism economy, and concentrates the administration of the national employment-quota law for travesti, trans and transgender people alongside the national femicide/travesticide registry — it is where state response is most likely to be present. Against that: on 18 September, six months after an unlawful detention, officers from police station 18 carried out fresh detentions, arrests and arbitrary identifications of travestis and trans women in the Constitución neighbourhood, writing several up under article 81 of the City's Contravention Code for lacking documents and arresting one — activists describe it as 'a new illegal procedure against travestis and trans', the third-plus iteration of the same operation in the same barrio, making it a pattern rather than a single incident. Nationally the climate has turned: 2025 set a record of at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity (+62% on 2024, one every 38 hours, the highest since monitoring began ten years ago), 32% of them inside police stations and penal facilities, with security-force violence multiplying from 17 cases (2024) to 64 (2025), trans women and travestis the majority of victims (142, 62.5%); federal closures of the equality ministry and the national anti-discrimination institute and dismissals of trans public-sector quota hires further erode recourse.

sources.summary: Washington Blade (10 April 2025): Argentine trans and travesti activists at a CABA rights forum (4 April 2025) describe their community's situation under the current administration as 'chaotic, desperate', with growing fear and vulnerability to violence, discrimination and poverty; the administration eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry in December 2023, closed the national anti-discrimination institute (INADI) in 2024, and dismissed trans people the government had hired under the Trans Labor Quota Law (1% of public-sector posts). Named association honours Diana Sacayán, a trans activist stabbed to death in her Buenos Aires apartment in 2015, and Lohana Berkins, who died in 2016.

Agencia Presentes (19 March 2026), National Hate Crime Observatory data: 2025 was a record year — at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity, +62% on the previous year, one every 38 hours (highest since monitoring began ten years ago); perpetrators were mostly security-force members and unknown individuals in public spaces, with beating the most used modality; security-force violence cases multiplied from 17 (2024) to 64 (2025); 32% of 2025's crimes occurred in police stations and penal facilities (including a violent raid on a prison diversity pavilion that injured over 45 LGBT+ people and eight guards detained for beating a trans inmate); trans women and travestis were 62.5% of victims (142 cases); 64.8% of cases (147) were physical assaults (+101%), the remainder lethal — 16 murders (10 trans women), 53 structural-violence deaths and 11 suicides; in January 2025 a known stalker burned the home of lesbian activists, and a 55-year-old teacher was murdered in the Caballito neighbourhood in circumstances bearing hate-crime features the media did not frame as such.
